claims.text: A machine-learning model integrating classical phonon-scattering theories with descriptors of atomic size mismatch and mixing entropy will predict low phonon thermal conductivity in homogenized FCC high-entropy alloys more accurately than existing isotropic models.
Arc melting followed by homogenization at approximately 1200 °C for 24 hours ensures a uniform, solid-solution state in CoCrFeMnNi.
The proposed framework incorporates statistical descriptors of atomic disorder into modified classical phonon-scattering models.
The proposed measurements cover room temperature through 600 K.
Multicomponent atomic disorder characterized by atomic-size mismatch and mixing entropy produces lattice distortions.
The lattice distortions associated with multicomponent disorder enhance phonon scattering.
Intrinsic disorder in FCC high-entropy alloys enhances phonon scattering.
Intrinsic disorder in FCC high-entropy alloys reduces effective phonon group velocity.
Quantifying atomic disorder with statistical descriptors enables a better correlation between atomic-level disorder and macroscopic thermal conductivity.
The integrated model will reduce thermal-conductivity prediction error by more than 20% relative to conventional isotropic models.
Computed disorder metrics will show a clear correlation with measured low phonon thermal conductivity.
Current isotropic phonon-scattering models do not explicitly account for atomic-size mismatch or mixing entropy.
Current isotropic models exhibit larger deviations from laser-flash experimental data than the proposed model is expected to exhibit.
The proposed model is applicable only to well-homogenized, single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys without significant grain-size variation.
The model's accuracy outside the stated single-phase, homogeneous FCC domain remains untested.
Minor segregation or secondary-phase formation may affect the quantitative improvement and applicability of the model.

The hypothesis is falsified if model predictions deviate by more than 15% from measured thermal conductivity or if disorder descriptors lack a statistically significant correlation with thermal conductivity.
